topic.name: Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 0 & 36 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=6$ and $\sigma_2=0.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=36,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A -36 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 36 \end{bmatrix} - 36 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -36 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 36I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 0 & 36 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0& 36 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 0I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the matrix $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ V = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=5$ and $\sigma_2=4.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

A - 25 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 25 & 0 \\ 0 & 16 \end{bmatrix} - 25 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 25I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=16,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 16 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 25 & 0 \\ 0 & 16 \end{bmatrix} - 16 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 16I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the matrix $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0\\0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 10 \\ 10 & 14 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=2\sqrt{6}$ and $\sigma_2=2.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=24,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 24 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -10 \\ 10 & 14 \end{bmatrix} - 24 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & 10 \\ 10 & -10 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 24I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=4,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 4 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 10 \\ 10 & 14 \end{bmatrix} - 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 10 \\ 10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 4I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the matrix $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: Finding the Third Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=\sqrt{10}$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

\[ \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix} \]

such that $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1.$

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} x_2 + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-x_2 + 2x_3 = 0}, \] we get the general solution

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_1} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{2x_3} \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = x_1 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_1} + x_3 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_2}, \]

where $x_1$ and $x_3$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \end{bmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}} \end{bmatrix} \]

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following: \[ U = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=5\sqrt{2}$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{4}{5\sqrt{2}}} \\ \dfrac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

\[ \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix} \]

such that $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1.$

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ \dfrac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} x_1 + \dfrac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} x_2 + \dfrac{3}{5\sqrt{2}} x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{4x_1 + 5x_2 + 3x_3 = 0}, \] we get the general solution

\[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_2} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{4}{3}x_1 - \dfrac{5}{3}x_2} \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{3}x_1 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_1} + \dfrac{1}{3}x_2 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_2}, \]

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ are not mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let \[ \mathbf{c}_1=\mathbf{b}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Then, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c}_2 &= \mathbf{b}_2 - \dfrac{\mathbf{b}_2 \cdot \mathbf{c}_1}{\mathbf{c}_1 \cdot \mathbf{c}_1}\mathbf{c}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{20}{25} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{3}{5} \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{5} \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{5}} \\ 0 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{4}{5}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{5}{5\sqrt{2}}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{3}{5\sqrt{2}}} \end{bmatrix} \]

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following: \[ U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{3}{5} & -\dfrac{4}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \dfrac{5}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{3}{5\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{4}{5} & -\dfrac{3}{5\sqrt{2}} \\ \end{bmatrix} \]
